utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning. Joanna Korner, Alexis Demirdjian, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, and Maggie di Gaudio appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. We have been alerted that there's a matter which the Defence wished to raise. But before we hear from that, there is the matter of -- I believe there are two documents which the translation -- two documents on which the Zupljanin Defence which they wish to use, the translations of which have not been completed. First of all, what is the update on the status of those translations? And the question that we have for the Prosecution arising out of that is whether they are content with the drafts which I understand have been provided. Could we hear from Mr. Krgovic as to where we are with the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We are in correspondence with the service and we were told that the translation would arrive this week, but we did not receive a specific date in respect of the whole translation. We were only told that it is due to be finished this week, and I'm talking about the expert report of General Kovacevic. We have received a draft translation. And my Case Manager is in contact with the CLSS and we do expect it to be resolved very soon. As soon as we receive any sort of information, we will inform both the Chamber and the OTP through our Legal Assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There is, of course, the procedural matter that at this point you are not in compliance with the extant order of the Chamber in this regard. But anyway, let me hear from the OTP. Sorry, were you about to respond to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Since we are waiting for the translation of the footnotes as well, we are cross-referencing our references with what is in the law library in order to place all the additional documents on our 65 ter list. But since we don't have all the documents yesterday, we were unable to honour the Trial Chamber's order. Therefore we will ask to have a meeting with the CLSS today and we will report back to the Chambers on it and, if necessary, ask for any extension of the dead-line for the submission of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So do I understand the position to be that you are waiting to formalize your application until you are in a position to intelligently say what the application is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Since we haven't received a clear answer from the translation service as to when the translation would be finished, we can't give you our exact position as to what our application for an extension of the dead-line would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I say this, we haven't the slightest interest in working on a draft report which may change, but equally, we're not taking any point on the delay on the basis that we're not likely to get to Mr. Krgovic's expert before July at the earliest, even longer if we go on like the way we're going at the moment. So we're not taking any point on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yesterday during the examination-in-chief of our first witness, the Prosecution sent us a list of the documents they intend to use during their cross-examination of the same witness. To our great surprise, I must say, we found, late in the afternoon and during the night, that a number of documents have never been disclosed to us. I will give you a list of these documents, but I'd like first to explain what the situation involves. First off, the Rules are quite clear and there's no reason for me to try and expound on them, either for the benefit of the Chamber or my learned friends who are well acquainted with it. The disclosure obligation lies on the Prosecution. We also have the jurisprudence both of this Tribunal and the Rwanda Tribunal, which I need not cite, but it is quite clear in its position as to the OTP obligation to disclose materials. The placement of documents into the EDS system does not mean by no account that the OTP thus fulfills its obligation to disclose material. On Monday, the Chamber requested that we provide copies of the interview our client had with the Prosecution. We did so. And only after we had done so we received information from the Prosecution that the entire transcript is in fact in existence of his interview from 2009. We had asked for it on the 26th of May, 2009. We had asked for the entire transcript of Mr. Bjelosevic's interview to be provided to us. At 16.45 of the day before his arrival we finally received them. You'll recall that in January we lost at least two hours of court time, and I don't know how many hours that my team had to spend working, on the documents referenced in the book by Colonel Lisica, and it was only yesterday that we received, on the same list of the Prosecution, one of the documents from the same book that they were given by this witness who has taken the stand now back in 2004. I am terribly concerned about the situation, I must say so. We have now received documents that we have never seen before, that we have never been able to discuss with our witness, because we didn't know that they existed. Apparently the Prosecution has had them all along. These are not documents that were obtained yesterday or that they received at some point. From the 28th of March earlier this year, when we filed our 65 ter list, the OTP knew that our first witness would be Mr. Bjelosevic. And it was during the interview in 2009 that Mr. Bjelosevic mentioned the fact that he was called to be a Defence witness. Since this is our first witness, Your Honours, we really have to insist on the application of Rule 68 bis and that pursuant to that Rule the Prosecution be adequately sanctioned for the failure to disclose material. If this is the situation we are encountering at the very beginning, who knows what will happen when our other witnesses follow. If we are always going to receive documentation only after our witnesses have taken their oath, it seems to me that there will be none of the fair trial that we are due. I will now list the relevance documents. And I can reference them by tabs, rather than 65 ter numbers, that the Prosecution has given them yesterday. These are tabs 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 16, 17, 23, 28, 30, 34, 69, 72, 86, 87, 88, 90, 97. Your Honours, I have the entire documentation containing all our requests and the responses from the Prosecution, and if the Prosecution should deny any of what we've said, we can provide this for the benefit of the Chamber. Now, the Rules we invoke are Rule 66, and the jurisprudence is the Lukic and Lukic case, decision on Milan Lukic's motion to suppress, et cetera, the 3rd of November, 2008. Rule 68, the decision of the Trial Chamber in the Karadzic case, 10th of March, 2009. The Miroslav Bralo case of 30th of August, 2006. And the decision in the Prosecutor versus Karamira case, the Appeals Chamber decision of the 30th of June, 2006. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for I don't know how many times, and I would deplore the bringing up of these matters and quoting of authorities without advance notice to the Prosecution, notice of this application was made at -- to us by e-mail at 7.30 a.m. And I don't know about anybody else but I'm not in the habit of reading my e-mails at 7.30 in the morning. Your Honours, we obviously can deal with this very briefly now, but in the light -- as the Defence have mentioned a number of authorities and the like, we would wish to give a reasoned reply at a later stage. Your Honours, with regard, I can, however, deal with two matters. The complaint about the transcript of the interview. Can I start by pointing out that this witness has never been on our witness list and was never on our witness list. He was one of many, many senior officials with the Serbian MUP whom the Office of the Prosecutor interviewed, some of whom were put on to the list of witnesses to be called and some who were not. Many of these witnesses told us that they had been approached by the Defence, which in our view was neither here nor there. The vast majority of those who had told us they had been approached by the Defence are not on the Defence witness list. Your Honours may have been somewhat surprised, as, I have to confess, we were, at the paucity of witnesses who were coming to speak about those events. Your Honours, in respect of this witness, we -- he was interviewed originally in 2004 and then interviewed again in 2009, and he did, like, as I say, many others witnesses tell us that he had been approached to be a Defence witness. He said he was asked if he had made a statement to the Defence and he said no he hadn't, as I recall. I haven't checked that recently. We only had part -- can I say, Your Honours, straightaway: We disclosed both those interview, the tapes thereof, in full virtually from the 2004 one, when disclosure began, to the 2009 in a matter of days, I believe. We therefore fulfilled our obligations entirely under Rule 68. The only obligation that we had to disclose any of that interview was Rule 68, which we did. In fact, we went further than our obligations because we gave them the whole interview, whereas we could have simply extracted from it the Rule 68 material. So it is misleading to inform Your Honours that we had withheld from the Defence this interview. We only had part of it transcribed because that was the part that was of interest to us, which dealt with the Mice in Teslic. At a later stage, after the Defence request, we had a number of other interviews transcribed on the basis we were not sure, and in anticipation, of whom the Defence might be calling. And we also had that one, the whole interview, as opposed to the excerpt transcribed. We gave them the excerpt out of the kindness of our collective hearts, not because we were obliged to. And, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, where did you disclose these interviews?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honours give me one moment, I'll just ask Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we disclosed the whole tape on the 8th of July, 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And how? By sending the tapes to the Defence or by putting it on the EDS? Or how?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, no, no, we sent them. We put everything onto DVD or CD that we disclosed. No, no, we don't -- if we disclose, we don't say, Go and look for it in EDS. It wouldn't be on EDS, in any event. But, Your Honours, this complaint, we say, is without any merit whatsoever. We did, then, for our own purposes get it transcribed. And it's absolutely right they asked us whether we'd had the whole part transcribed and we said no just the part we disclosed to them. After it had been transcribed, I'm afraid to say that in the many, many requests and things that were happening in this case, I forgot that we had it until I saw -- may I say, I explained all this in an e-mail to Ms. Savic, so I'm somewhat surprised to have it raised like this. When we saw them uploading the interview which said "partial," we then remembered that we had the whole one. And, though, as I say, we have no obligation whatsoever to help them out, their calling this witness, they should have actually had the rest of the interview transcribed or asked us if we'd had it done, but they didn't. So, Your Honours, we then -- we gave them the transcript and that's how it's been uploaded. So, Your Honours, I take grave exception to that complaint. Your Honours, as regards the second part of the complaint, namely that there are documents on our list to ask Mr. Bjelosevic about which are not -- have not been disclosed, apart from the fact that some of them are already on the Defence list and exhibited by them, but, Your Honours, as I say, I've been taken by surprise by this. I haven't had an opportunity to look at the authorities that Mr. Zecevic has just reeled of off his head nor checked the correspondence with the Defence because our obligation to disclose, after 66 -- Rule 66(A) has been complied with, is if there's a request under 66(B) or if it contains 68. And, Your Honours, as far as we're concerned, certainly none of the material we're going to use is Rule 68. The query is, Does it come under Rule 66 B? Firstly, I need to check the Defence request; second, I need to look at the authorities. And so at this point in time, Your Honour, I'm not in a position to deal with this, but can do tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So there the matter would rest until the Prosecution is able to formulate a full response to the matter raised by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If there is nothing else, may the usher please escort the witness to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bjelosevic. You may be seated. You may take your seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The practice is that at the beginning of each day's sitting I would remind the witness that he is still on his oath, that is, the solemn declaration that he would have made at the -- before he began his testimony. But I was reminded that something -- that there's something I neglected to do yesterday which I'm about to do now, but before I do that, let me state clearly that nothing that I am about to say suggests that the Chamber has any questions about the veracity or otherwise of anything you would have said so far. We are not at that stage in terms of the deliberative duty which the Chamber would have. But it is something of which I should have pointed out to you when you made the solemn declaration yesterday and it is this: That the solemn declaration, which I'm sure that you recall, the usher would have handed to you on a card, is not a mere ritual or formality; it imposes upon a witness, such as yourself, an obligation to give truthful testimony before this Tribunal. And should you fail to do so, this Tribunal is empowered under the Statutes which constitute it to impose penalties for perjury, that is, for giving false or misleading testimony. So that is something which, as I said, I should have pointed out at the very beginning yesterday. And to come back to what I said at the begin, we begin a new day, and I remind you of the solemn declaration. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Bjelosevic, given that we followed a chronological order, yesterday we came to the beginning of 1992. Tell me, please, are you aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I see that the witness doesn't have his binder with documents here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please turn to tab 16. 776D1. And please comment on it if you are familiar with the event.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am familiar with the document and I also know about the event described here. Namely, the bridge between the Bosnian -- Bosanski and Slavonski Samac was indeed mined, and this is a dispatch that Minister Delimustafic sent to the addresses listed here, that is to say, to the Crisis Staff of Slavonski Brod municipality. However, I don't know whether this is really a standard routine type of correspondence; I'm not sure about that. But I am familiar with the case. I know about this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you're not sure that this is a standard routine, the typical correspondence, would you please explain it to us.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the level. Since this involves the Crisis Staff of the Slavonski Brod municipality, then it should have been considered as a local level. And for a minister, a member of the cabinet, to get involved in something like this, well, he normally corresponds with people who are his equals, in terms of level. But let me tell you something else: There was a request from the Croatian side. Such requests mostly came from Slavonski Brod. And the request was for the JNA, which, to remind you, was the legal armed force of the SFRY, to be withdrawn 25 kilometres south of the Sava River. Such request was made with a view to create a solid whole, a solid entity, on both banks of the Sava River, on the right and on the left bank. This is why they pressured for the joint mixed check-points to be withdrawn. The destruction of the bridge, which until the very end remained unclear in terms of the perpetrator, should also be viewed as a way to pressure the Bosnian side, to make the Bosnian side also request the withdrawal of the JNA 25 kilometres to the south of the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These facts, the destruction of this bridge and some other destructions that we saw earlier, the requests for the JNA to be withdrawn 25 kilometres from the border into the depth of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did it affect the population in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in that region, and if so, to what extent?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it affected them. Most of the population of Croat and Muslim ethnicity supported the request, at least those who were in Bosanski Brod and parts of Derventa. As for the Serbs, almost 100 per cent of them. A large number of Muslims and a large number of Croats living in Derventa and to the south, they supported the presence of the JNA, seeing them as the federal force which provided security to all citizens and all nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there are objections, I would like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I ask for the original, please. The photocopy is so bad that it's impossible to see what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we received this document from the section of criminal defence with the state court in Sarajevo. This and the next document were received from them, and this is a copy of the document which can be found in the State Court for War Crimes of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And these are all of the documents that we have from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'd like to see the original, please. As I say, at the moment, Your Honours, I'm afraid it is almost impossible to tell what this document is. It's not signed, it's not stamped, at least as far as I can tell. And so until such time as we have a better copy, I'm saying it should be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, apart from the provenance issue which Ms. Korner has raised, the -- apart from the historical curiosity about this incident, how is it relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, maybe the witness should take his earphones off. [Interpretation] Switch off your mike, please. [In English] Well, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Incidentally, I wonder whether the witness understands English. Because yesterday there was a -- I remember that he had responded before that there -- but anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like to know that as well, actually, Your Honour. Because otherwise this is a pointless exercise and he will have to leave court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, but we can -- you can ask the witness, Your Honour. Or maybe I can ask the witness, whatever pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, do you speak -- do you understand English? Mr. Bjelosevic, the question is: To what extent, if any, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very little. Good afternoon, how do you do, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I take them off?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe this document is relevant because we have subsequent documents which will show that there was -- that there was a specific issue concerning the blowing up of the bridge in Bosanski Samac. And despite the fact that it was on the territory of the CSB and apparently under the jurisdiction of this witness, the conduct of the investigation was done completely without his knowledge or his made aware of the results of the commission that went on that. Therefore, it is also significant for the fact that the Minister Delimustafic communicates directly with the Crisis Staff of the Slavonski Brod, which is a Crisis Staff of the HDZ in Croatia, and therefore it only fits into the -- into the picture which we are trying to establish concerning the situation and our theory of the context why and for which reasons this witness, among others, went to the 11th of February meeting in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So is the -- should this document be marked for identification pending the resolution of the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I don't -- we have -- in the documents which the Office of the Prosecutor gave to us and which are admitted as the exhibits, a number of them are not signed, a number of them are not originals, and I don't see how we can apply the very new standard now when the Defence case is in question. We -- I gave the explanation of the provenance of the document. The provenance of the document, it comes from the State Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I received it from the office of the criminal defence, which is a part of the structure of the State Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the document I received is exactly this document, which I copied and provided the copy to the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm -- I don't know if the original exists at all. This is the copy which I received. And as far as I can help the Trial Chamber and anybody else, this is the document that -- that we received. Among other things, this is a telegram, and you -- we have at least 400 exhibits and telegrams which are not signed. It's just that the name is printed of the sender of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, firstly, we have nothing to say that this is a telegram because the whole of the top part has been cut off. Your Honours, it's incumbent upon the Defence to have a legible original if they want to exhibit a document. At the moment, we simply don't even know what this is. There's nothing to show that it was sent. If anything, it looks more as it comes out of a book. We're back to that one again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, Ms. Korner, the notion of best evidence means best obtainable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but they can go back to the state court and say, Send us a proper copy. Not this. And if that's all that exists, well then they can say so. But at the moment they haven't checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it is my understanding that this is what exists in the state court and there is no other better copy than this. And among other things, it has on it DD and everything else, and it's obvious that it's -- that the document is a telegram.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, can I say, the original, if you look, it says 1/2. I rather feel this comes out, it may be not a book or something like that, but something else. I don't think a telegram, if this was the original or even a copy of the original, would have 1/2 like that. If Your Honours can't -- you will have to have a look at the next -- sorry, I've got the -- it's photocopied on two pages for us. You haven't seen the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, how come on the English translation there is, on the top of the first page, information, socialist republic, et cetera, which you can't see on the copy, on the copy and on the monitor, in the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if we can have back the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is there. In the right -- right-hand corner, it says "MUP SRBiH/10 DD," and that is exactly what is the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So the original copy you have is as bad as the copy you gave to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's my ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, they gave us -- can I -- "gave" is not the right word. When their list of documents produced on Friday night, this was uploaded into e-court, we've not seen this before, or the vast majorities of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was disclosed to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm being told that it was when they gave the 65 ter list, so I take that back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we see the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D448 [Realtime transcript read in error "148"], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it can't be 148.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the transcript says "148," so ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The correct number is 448, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, can we now take the document. Let's look at the document at tab 25, 789D1. And I would like to invite your comments, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a dispatch that I myself sent to the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in this dispatch I asked them to inform us as a service, as well as the general public, as to who had destroyed the bridge. Our team from the CSB Doboj carried out an on-site investigation. However, the investigation proper was taken over by a team from the BiH MUP. Therefore, we were not able to carry out other own investigation. We were not able to establish who had destroyed the bridge. That's why I asked them to provide us with information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You sent this dispatch to the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there are objections, I would like to tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What is the ... yes, I see it. Sorry, Your Honour, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was merely going to say that we will take all of the previous discussions from this morning and indeed yesterday about relevance as being incorporated into this, and the document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D449, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, could you now look at 780D1 at tab 19.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat? The interpretation was still going on, so I couldn't hear you. Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, are we still on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, not anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then I would like to ask the witness whether he got that report he asked for and whether he knows who were the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the witness, in his previous, he said, We were never made aware who was ... in his previous answer. That is why I didn't ask further. In his previous answer, he -- I believe he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: As I understood it, his answer was: And that's why we asked the minister to report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please comment on this document.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is another dispatch that I sent again. I sent again because I had already sent such dispatches to the minister, his deputy, and the chief of the police administration. What I requested in the dispatch was for them to stop engaging in parallel dealings in the municipalities of Bosanski Brod and Samac because as you can see from the things that were previously said, we were prevented from even carrying out an ordinary investigation. They had almost fully taken over the management of the service in the area in Bosanski Brod and in Bosanski Samac, that is. They selected policemen for the service and brought them from outside. At the same time, the responsibility for the situation in the area lay with the CSB Doboj. That's why I asked for those practices to be discontinued, so as to allow us to carry out our duties properly at the CSB. This pattern of behaviour, which started with the inspectors, was transferred on to the chief of the station in Bosanski Samac. He also pushed out the commander from the system of command and control. On several occasion, the commander addressed me and complained about the problems that he had encountered. The chief of the station deployed a policeman on the ground; at the same time, the commander was only required to put his signature on the fait accompli. He himself had not participated in anything. Later on, and even then at this time, there were information and it became clear why those two police stations should have been placed under the control of those inspectors. Those were the axes along which equipment and weapons were being transported for the paramilitary units in the central part of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This dispatch was sent to the minister, the deputy minister, and to somebody marked as 01. What is 01?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the police administration, the administration for the uniformed police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there are objections, I would like to tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D450.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You have just mentioned a letter or, rather, information that you received from the commander of the Bosanski Samac Police Station. Could you please look at tab 28, 793D1. Look at it, and then I would like to invite your comments on it.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a dispatch which was sent by the commander of the Bosanski Samac Police Station. His name was Mr. Jekic. In this dispatch, he informed the MUP headquarters. I believe that the number 10 is the office of the minister, 01 is the administration for the police, and then there are different departments after the slashes. And then he also copied me as the security service centre in Doboj, to me as its chief, and to its various departments. This is his resignation. He says that he can no longer perform his duties. He can no longer do his job because of the wilfulness of Chief Dragicevic, because Chief Dragicevic simply left out all the other commanders from the processes of decision-making, and, as you can see here, he says that Dragicevic does not call sessions of his expert team, although he should, in order to discuss matters and analyse the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does this document tie in with your previous answer or, rather, the answer to my previous question when you mentioned problems in Bosanski Samac; is that it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. This is precisely the document that confirms my previous answer. As I've told you, he called me on the phone several times, but I was powerless there because Dragicevic received his orders from the inspectors, and very often he didn't even reply to my telephone calls.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say those inspectors from which he received orders, if I understand you properly, you meant the inspectors who had been sent from the MUP unbeknownst to you and without your consent?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Hodzic and the one who replaced him later. There were always two inspectors down there, those that had been sent by Mr. Panjeta, but they often changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, unless there are objections, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D451, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at 782D1, tab 20. And again, could you comment on it.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a dispatch that I signed and sent to the minister of the interior, Delimustafic, deputy minister, and the administration of the police, and the administration for the detection and prevention of crimes. It had become very obvious that the existing system or the system that was legally provided for, the system of control and command in the service, had been destroyed or suspended at the moment when those inspectors were sent out. We had somebody in Bosanski Brod and Bosanski Samac at all times, Omer Stambolic and, if I remember properly, Petar Amas [phoen] changed places in those cities all the time. They were covered by the inspectors, and those inspectors were contrary to the system that was in place. They had contacts with the parties, with the SDA and the HDZ. They also maintained contacts in the service exclusively with the members of the Muslim and Croatian ethnicity, be it commanders, deputies, or chiefs, and they drafted their own reports, their own information, that they sent out and we had never had an opportunity to discuss those reports that were sent out. And we could all see where that was going and what that was in service of. And as I told you, that part of the Sava valley, or Posavina, as it is known, was being tied to the organs in Croatia in the municipality of Slavonski Brod. And on the other hand, things were being put in place to organise paramilitary units under the auspices of the SDA. And that's what was done in the territory of the municipalities of Doboj, Tesanj, Maglaj, and at that time we already had very reliable information and data about what was going on and what formations had already been established by that time and what weapons had already been distributed to them by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you send your reports to the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as was, I presume, your duty under the laws and regulations in place?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course. We had a constant flow of reports from our premises, as well as reports on security information. The same applied to both public and state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And were you privy to reports sent by those inspectors to the MUP? You said that these matters were not discussed, but did -- were you privy to those?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said that they drafted reports that they sent out without consulting any of the people in any leading positions there, and I said that I didn't know what they were sending out and that I was trying to get in touch with them, both in writing and over the phone, trying to let them know and reason with them that whatever we were doing in that area had to be done jointly. But it never came to us consulting, assessing, or deciding on anything together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With this particular dispatch, did you request anything of them or did you make any suggestions or indications as to what your next steps would be?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see there at the very end that I said that should this practice continue, I would inform thereof the relevant authorities, the general public, the federal SUP, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask for a meeting with the leadership of the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was on several occasions that I asked for a meeting with the Minister Delimustafic, either over the telephone, by talking to the secretary, or in the letters that I wrote them, but I never, in fact, ended up meeting with the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The document itself says, I'm asking for the meeting, so that's why I was leading the question. To save time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The proper question, and you saw me get to my feet, is: What did you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will try my best. Thank you. If there is no -- I would like to admit this document if there's no opposition to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like to know if the original, which is not a very good copy, has a date. And if not - I assume this is a document this witness provided - could he tell us what the date is, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, can you give us the date of the document, or roughly the period?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't date the document, but I think it was in late February or early March that this happened. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, at the top, but it's so bad, the copy, you can't see it, I want to know if the witness can tell us, because, as I say, I assume he produced this document, what's on the top of it, who -- what signature it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe it can be enlarged on the monitor so witness can comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The initials up there probably belong to the individual who forwarded the dispatch. As for what is up at the top, it's the date or the time when the dispatch was sent out and the reference number it was assigned. It's the number in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, is this your dispatch, and do you know if it was sent to the MUP at all?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it was sent to the MUP. And I was explaining what it is that we can see in the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, isn't this, as for documents I mean, isn't this getting repetitive?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it helps, I will -- we will accept, on behalf of the Prosecution, that Mr. Bjelosevic complained for a number of months to the MUP or officials of the MUP about things he said were not being done properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- I don't know whether I properly understood Ms. Korner's statement just now to mean that this acceptance - I was going to use the word "concession," but I would use the vague word "acceptance" - means that it isn't necessary, in the Prosecution's view, for more documents of this repetitive nature to be overlaid before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that's a matter for you and for Mr. Zecevic. I'm simply pointing out that I'm certainly not going to dispute that this witness complained on a number of occasions about things that he said were not being done properly. Whether his complaints are justified or not is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's -- maybe the witness can -- [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, can you take your headphones off and the microphones. [In English] Your Honours, the point of the matter is exactly this: First of all, whether it was justified, it is for Your Honours to decide. Now, I'm trying to show you, because our position is that his complaints were more than justified because he is actually repeating and repeating and asking and asking and he doesn't get the proper response from the ministry as he should have. That's one thing. The second thing, Your Honours: This document is after the 11th of February. Therefore, the suggestion of the Office of the Prosecutor or their theory that the 11th of February means that the ultimate decision to split the MUP and that Serbian MUP will have nothing to do with the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina anymore is clearly wrong, because he, Mr. Bjelosevic, who was there, who discussed on that meeting like you will see in a second, is now asking again Minister Delimustafic and is bringing to his attention the wrong-doings, the problems, and he's asking a meeting with Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Point taken, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that is not a proper or accurate description of what we say about the 11th of February meeting, but Your Honours will hear what I have to say when we get to cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D452, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My apologies, I forget. Can you hear me? Can you hear me now? No.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I can hear properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, did you attend a meeting in Banja Luka, and, if so, can you tell us when this was and what the reason for it was and what the subject of discussions at this meeting was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are you now going to the meeting on 11th of February?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please would -- because then I would like to ask the witness a question before we come to the meeting of 11th February. Because, Mr. Bjelosevic, I would like to know, if you can tell us, what was your interpretation of the fact that the MUP in Sarajevo, under Alija Delimustafic's orders, was sending out inspectors who interfered with the ordinary work of the SJBs in Doboj and indeed in the CSB of Doboj itself? What did you think was going on, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Frankly speaking, to this day I'm not clear on whether this was Minister Delimustafic's decision or whether all these matters ended up with Mr. Pusina, because I had never seen a dispatch signed by Mr. Delimustafic on this issue, or, rather, I have never received one. Jusuf Pusina sent out a dispatch after two or three interventions on my part asking to be told what these individuals were doing, but I sent my letters every time to the minister's office. Now, generally speaking, as for these inspectors being sent to Doboj, Bosanski Brod, and Bosanski Samac, my understanding was that this was in the service of preparing, organising, and creating certain paramilitary units which would subsequently, in part, become the BH army and in part would come under the command of the ministry in Sarajevo, because the normal workings of a service out in the field, especially once those check-points were set up under check-point 91 operation, would not allow for such practices. There were instances where people bent on sabotage were stopped, I think it was in Brcko and elsewhere, and they were found to have explosives on them. And in the area of the CSB Doboj, our traffic police stops a vehicle that was on its way there from Germany and which was under police escort. It was packed full of military equipment. Now that I've mentioned this, let me say that from that point when the police stopped this vehicle, we, and when I say "we," I mean the CSB of Doboj, were imposed some sort of sanctions. The regular supplies, with vehicles, radio sets, weapons, and other equipment, although planned, stopped at that point. This was another subject of my complaints, repeated complaints, because none of the equipment that we were due was forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you had the suspicion that the Muslims were secretly organising paramilitary units who at one point would seek to take over command in Doboj and the surrounding SJBs; is that a correct interpretation of what you have told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The only difference being that this wasn't based on suspicions or doubt. It was based on verified information about the goings on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This raises two questions to me. First of all, what did you do to counter this development? And, secondly, how or why did this involve the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then let me first start from the latter then. At a time of election campaigns, the HDZ and SDA attended rallies together as a coalition, and at some of these rallies their two flags would even be tied up together symbolically. This was to serve as a symbol of their unity. And these circles had roughly the same objective, namely to break up the former Yugoslavia. Now, what is it that I and the service did? We provided regular information on all these events that we learned of, and that was the extent of what we were able to do. The information was sent to the Ministry of the Interior. When federal inspectors were present in our area, we told them what we knew about what was going on as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We may get back to this at a later point. I notice the time, so maybe this is an appropriate moment to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in relation to the discussion we had this morning, I would like to tell the Court that we have just received the translation of the expert report by General Kovacevic and it will be uploaded as we speak and made available to all parties. What remains now is to translate some 20 footnotes. And according to the CLSS, that should be completed by the end of the week. So that all of the documents that are mentioned in the footnotes will be also uploaded into e-court before the end of the week and thus made available to all parties as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you for the update, Mr. Krgovic. Yes, could we have the witness back on the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we're just waiting for the witness to come in, Your Honours yesterday raised the question of an e-mail circulating about sitting times once Your Honours' other case starts. At the moment nobody seems to have got any e-mail, either us or the Defence, about that. All we -- I see everybody shaking their head. Obviously it would help from our points of view, particularly, I imagine, from Mr. Zecevic's point of view, to know well in advance what is proposed by the Court as to the sitting. From our point of view, I think it makes more sense to have a block devoted to one case rather than, say, two days on one, two days on other, but that may not be what the Defence want. But anyhow, I think it would help if we could be told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, the -- when I mention -- well, first of all, obviously I took advantage of the opportunity to alert counsel as early as possible to this, and the notion of an e-mail was what a our understanding, as the Judges, were that the -- at the level of the SLOs, that they were going to generate this, and by that means involve counsel in the two related cases. So I just assumed that this had been initiated, but I had no reason to follow-up on where this was. The Judges have discussed the possibility; they have their views. But obviously this will -- the final determination will depend on the views that counsel may have in terms of the proposals. So these -- it's relatively -- I was about to say it's relatively early yet, but then I'm reminded we're in the middle of April so it isn't as early as I think, but clearly it's a matter which is going to have to be resolved well in advance of June. But I could make inquiries as to the status of the communication and see where we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that would be very helpful. And can I just, say after many years at this Tribunal, I'm sure that Defence counsel will endorse the fact that it is never safe to assume anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was my understanding that Judge Harhoff was having some other questions. I'm perfectly willing to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: There may be one little question that I still would wish to raise with the witness before we come to the meeting of the 11th of February. And my question relates to the link between the facts that you had about Muslims secretly building up armed units and the transportation of weapons from Germany and other places into Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did you understand these transports of weaponry to be linked to the Muslim build-up of paramilitary units in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let me remind you that at that time the Yugoslavia still existed as one whole country and the state security service was organised, existed at the federal level and at the level of the republics. Our operatives from the CSB Doboj received good intelligence from their contacts in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina; they knew very well what was going on. I have already described to you how the traffic police stopped a vehicle, and I know for a fact about that vehicle because it was said at the time that they had arrived from Germany with weaponry. They were under escort of police control from, I think, Posusje. The police patrol joined them in Samac; they escorted the vehicle all along on that itinerary until just before entering Doboj; they were stopped by our traffic police at the intersection in Seslije, where the roads from Bosanski Brod and Bosanski Samac converge and then continue jointly via Doboj. Since the transport involved military equipment, military police came to the scene shortly thereafter. They took over the vehicle. And the equipment and the police escorting the vehicle were taken to the pensioners centre, given dinner, and then released to go back to their home stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And these policemen who were escorting the vehicle, if I understand you correctly, they were Muslim policemen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember their ethnicity. But they wore proper uniforms. I think they were from Posusje. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, I mean, this is completely open. Does that mean that they -- these -- the escort -- the police escort could as well have been Serbian and the weaponry was meant to be delivered to the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because the driver driving that truck said for whom it was intended. The policemen could have been of any ethnicity, those who were assigned to that task, because they were not told what the vehicle contained and what the purpose was. I really don't remember their ethnicity or their names right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And to whom was the weaponry meant to be delivered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were to escort it to Sarajevo. That's what they said. The driver himself gave a statement later on. Since this involved military equipment, it was taken over by the military police and the JNA security organ. And they initiated proceedings subsequently because this came under their jurisdiction because it involved military equipment. As for the policemen, they returned to their home police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that. But I still do not fully understand how you could link the allegations that you have, that you had at the time, about Muslims building up secretly-armed units on the one hand, and then on the other hand this transport of weaponry into Bosnia, when apparently you're not sure about to whom this weaponry was supposed to be delivered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already told you that we had a number of pieces of information and this was all forwarded to the MUP in Sarajevo. We had various pieces of intelligence about paramilitary formations, where they were being established, their strength. And we also had information about where the weapons arrived. Some of this we learned subsequently. And in this particular case we knew as the weapons were being transported. Now, your question was how did I know, how did we know, whom this was intended for. Well, they talked to the driver. And once they took over the equipment and investigated, they subsequently informed us that this was intended for a unit of the SDA in Sarajevo. That's the information we received from them, from the army. And let me tell you this: Back at that time while the police still worked at the check-point in Bosanski Brod, we were informed that a vehicle was supposed to arrive from Slavonski Brod escorted by Mr. Delimustafic. And when the vehicle, indeed carrying Minister Delimustafic, arrived, the policemen didn't dare inspect either his vehicle or the vehicle following him once he showed his papers. We drafted an Official Note regarding this, but it's understandable; the policemen simply didn't dare inspect the minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you have any information that the opposite side, that is to say, the Serbs, were also trying to build up armed units and perhaps importing weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All three sides were arming themselves. That's a fact. However, the Serbian side responded en masse to the JNA mobilisation call. So during that time there were no units created on their side. But as for weapons being obtained illegally, that was a fact, yes. And we received information concerning that too. I have already mentioned to you yesterday, if you remember, that guards were being set up, and later on that escalated in numbers on all sides. However, when it comes to paramilitary formations, as I have told you, the Serbs mostly responded to the JNA mobilisation call-up, so they didn't create their own units, except for being part of those village guards, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think we should stop here. And I give the floor back to Mr. Zecevic. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, we need 1D135, tab 18. But before we turn to the document, let me remind you of the question that I have already put to you: Did you attend the meeting on the 11th of February in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document represents the minutes of that meeting, that's tab 18. Please go over the document and tell us whether you remember that the persons mentioned in the preamble really attended the meeting. Did you yourself attend, what was said at the meeting, and what did you yourself say at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the accurate list of attendees. I attend the meeting as well. At the meeting we discussed the problems related to the functioning of the MUP. To make it clearer: Since the system was, we can surely say that, already falling apart, there was mistrust, and the police and crime service had difficulties working on the ground because the citizens mistrusted them. And there was especially prominent mistrust between citizens of one ethnicity towards policemen who were of a different ethnicity. If we add to this situation another problem which is lack of equipment, which was quite apparent, and I've already described to you how that looked like, we did not receive any of the materiel that had been planned to be delivered to us. So when we take all of that into account, it is clear that we had serious problems working on the ground. At this meeting, as you can see, everybody took the floor, including me. My words are recorded here. All of the attendees mostly spoke about the problems due to either complete failure to function or poor functioning of the MUP. They mentioned the fact that the meetings were not held, collegium meetings were not held, between the minister and chiefs of centre, that equipment was being delivered to the stations selectively. And then it was concluded that it would be better to organise this service within the framework of what was to be called the Serbian MUP, but a functioning MUP, and to ensure, as you can see from the interventions of attendees, law and order, security of citizens - I emphasise "citizens" because that's what was said at the meeting - and property. If this MUP that was discussed was to have a prefix "Serbian" before it, that didn't mean that they would selectively implement the law, or act in a discriminatory manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, on page 2 and 3 of the Serbian version, we can see your intervention. And since this is an abbreviated version of your words, could you please confirm whether you spoke about this and whether you mentioned anything else. Please tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the essence of what I spoke about. Those were my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, do you remember if there were some conclusions reached at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And they were listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please repeat your answer. The interpreter didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, Yes, conclusions were reached and they are listed in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection was one of the conclusions that the positions reached at the 11th of February meeting should be notified to Minister Delimustafic and that the ministry should be given dead-lines within which the situation established to be irregular would be rectified?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To your recollection was there any mention of these positions and views that were established on the 11th of February meeting being notified to the general public through the media?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was a fully transparent public meeting and the general public was informed of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After the meeting, did the situation in the area of your CSB and did the relationship with Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the CSB Doboj change in any way?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The situation became complicated even further and nothing changed in terms of supplies arriving, save for the fact that letters were sent stating requests for supplies and no replies were received. Still, we did press on with the correspondence by sending various dispatches. What followed was continued at even more glaring violation of rules, regulations, and laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you a document behind tab 23, and the document is 786D1. This is a dispatch dated the 9th of March, 1992. There's a signature there and a typewritten name of Andrija Bjelosevic. Tell me, do you recall this dispatch; is it yours?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall this dispatch. It's mine. It's got my signature on it. At this time the situation was already dramatic; I think I can put it that way. By that time there had already been conflicts breaking out in Bosanski Brod. And I think it was between the 3rd and the 4th of March, there were people wounded by that time. I'd like to stress that on this occasion the public security station of Bosanski Brod was captured by paramilitary formations. The CSB Doboj received a great deal of information about it. The Hotel Arda [as interpreted] in Bosanski Brod, where this unit stationed by MUP was housed, was also surrounded. The personnel was disarmed. When the policemen noticed that the hotel was being surrounded, they took up arms; they wanted to mount resistance. But the then chief of the station, Zvonko Mertanovic [phoen], said that they should lay their weapons down and said, and I'm quoting his words, Those are our people. When the policemen laid down their weapons, masked individuals wearing balaclavas on their heads stormed into the hotel, disarmed them, and stripped them of all their equipment. And they had flak jackets, radio sets, rifles. They were stripped of it all but were given back their pistols ultimately. And they were ordered to go back to where they came from. This unit was under the command of Drago Gatisa [phoen], a police inspector in the security services centre in Bihac. They left Bosnia Brod at that point. As for the town itself, the public security station had been seized and taken over, as were many other key institutions by paramilitary formations from Slavonski Brod and from the area of the Bosanski Brod municipality. Moreover, I need to share with you an impression that I got at the time: First of all, this was obviously a deliberate surrender of both the unit and the station itself. All of these operations were directed by Avdo Hebib; he was in charge of it all. As for the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was customary for it to engage the services of special units in situations that were far less dramatic than this one. For instance, when there was a strike in the company called Focatrans, they were engaged. Whereas in this particular situation, no special police unit was sent out to prevent this from happening, from the violation of what is established in the system. And it was here that I was trying to prevent the conflict from escalating and becoming an all-out conflict. So I suggested that we form joint forces with the military organs, which would be capable under those circumstances of restoring law and order. Now, why these joint forces? If I can explain this. I've already said before that the Serbian population responded to call-ups from the JNA, and they trusted the Yugoslav People's Army. The other two ethnic communities were more confident with MUP and placed greater trust in them. It was for this reason that I suggested that mixed forces should be set up, which would work together to restore law and order. In the area of the municipality of Doboj - and this is not directly related to this dispatch, but I would like to corroborate what I'm saying - pursuant to a decision by the National Defence Council, such forces were indeed set up. These were mixed check-points. And the situation was pretty much stable under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, can we just clarify a few things that you stated in your answer. Was there a unit that the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time of these events in Bosanski Brod had deployed previously already in Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. This unit that I mentioned as having been disarmed in Hotel Sava, that was the unit that was there from before. However, Mr. Hebib and Mr. Matanovic as chief of station, and this is something that was clear for all to see and something that the policemen who were present in the area reported in their subsequent reports, they surrendered both the station and the unit to the members of these paramilitary formations. They practically didn't mount any resistance at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Two short questions: This unit, which was there, I suppose, as reinforcement or aid for the Bosnia Brod Police Station, was it set up by the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Avdo Hebib was the co-ordinator of that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, if you know, was this a multi-ethnic unit? What was its composition?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a multi-ethnic unit, but I can't give you the percentages. The unit wasn't under my control, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My final question on this: You, as chief of CSB, were you informed of the deployment of one such unit by the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina into a station that was within your area?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't informed about it by the MUP. I learned this when they arrived in Bosanski Brod and it was then that the station in Bosanski Brod put me on notice of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there are objection, can this document be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D453, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, to illustrate the situation in Bosanski Brod, I'll show you a document behind tab 24, 788D1. The date is the 12th of March, 1992. It's a statement by one Petar Duronjic, a citizen of Bosanski Brod, given to the Doboj CSB. Please tell me if you are familiar with the statement and if you know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the statement which was taken on the premises of CSB Doboj by Inspector Branislav Petricevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A moment, please. Can you tell us, Who was Branislav Petricevic? An inspector of what?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An inspector in the department for crime detection and Prevention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A moment, please. And his signature as well as signatures of other individuals can be found on the second page; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the documents and one of the stories told by a citizen in relation to the 3rd and 4th of March. People were fleeing Bosanski Brod en masse trying to find refuge because a wave of arrests of citizens of Serb ethnicity began and there were a number of citizens of Muslim ethnicity who were arrested as well and they were those who were of pro-Yugoslav orientation, as it were. And now that I've mentioned it, I'd like to cite a case involving Ismet Djuheric [phoen] whose house was attacked later on, I don't remember the date, where he and his wife and daughter resisted the attack in self-defence. Later on his brother was captured. The entire family had many troubles, but he managed to get out of the area; I think it was through his connections within the refinery that was there. People were abandoning their homes and properties, their jobs, trying to get themselves out of harm's way, whoever had the ability to do so. And it is only natural that they were very worried and concerned and upset. They were looking for help. However, by that time, Bosanski Brod had been blocked by these forces. And as is stated here, these were paramilitary formations, units of the National Guard's Corps, HOS, and some other local units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, just a few things. The gentleman that you have just mentioned, Ismet Djukalic [as interpreted], you said?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djukalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim, was he not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, according to what you know, since you know, you are familiar with the case, who was it that attacked his house when he had to defend himself together with his family?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paramilitary formations, the HOS members.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you just explain for all of us, What does HOS stand for?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time in 1992, in the month of March, you were familiar with this statement, you were familiar with the case of this Mr. Duronjic from Bosanski Brod; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there are objections, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We have reservations about how much of assistance this is, Mr. -- we have the witness's testimony relating these incidents -- this incident --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours. I understand. It's not important. I just wanted this document to illustrate the situation and confirm the words of the witness. But if Your Honours feel that it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We have his account.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, can I just -- can I just, again, just mention this: Again, how far is this going to go? This is not evidence relating to any municipalities on the indictment. I appreciate it's being adduced for the reasons that Mr. Zecevic has explained, but I do -- and this is not an in terrorem remark: It will be necessary to explore areas partially in cross, if this line of examination-in-chief is going on, which are completely outside the indictment, and I'm afraid that is the reality. And it's already happened, I'm afraid. So, I mean, I'm not quite clear on what basis Your Honours are accepting this kind of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you now look at document at tab 26, 787D1. Or rather, let's skip that document. I want to avoid any future objections of the same kind. Let's look at tab 27, document number 970D1 [as interpreted]. This is a dispatch dated 16 March 1992. It was sent to the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your name is typed up, and there's also a signature. Could you tell us whether this dispatch was sent by you, whether it was drafted by you, are you familiar with this dispatch? Did you send it to the MUP? What is the dispatch about?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I signed this dispatch. I'm familiar with the contents thereof. The situation on the ground was becoming dramatic and that's why I appealed and I urged all the concerned to proceed to set up the joint forces of the police and the army in order to put a stop to the war that was in the making, I dare say, by that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document or, rather, this dispatch, was it sent to the MUP? And who was the addressee, who received it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The addressee is the office of the minister; the police administration; the administration for crime detection and prevention; and then 05, which was the analytical service, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there are objections, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no objections. Query: Whose writing is on the document, please? And who did the crossings out?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, we can see that things were added by hand. Could you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that. When the dispatch was typed and brought to me for signature, I added these writings in order to highlight the urgency of the matter. I wanted everything to be done to prevent any further escalation of the situation. So these are my writings. I added that to the typed-up dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, sorry, and does that mean deleted the line that we can see as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I deleted the lines as well because I thought that the description of the area was irrelevant because the situation was getting to be more complicated in the entire area, across the board. I had created the document, I made changes to it, I deleted things from it, and then I signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one correction. It was recorded wrongly: The 65 ter number is 790D1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit 1D454.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, we have another document: 185D1 at tab 31. This is a dispatch sent on the 31st of March, 1992. Your name is typed up. But before that we have the word "Za," on behalf of the chief of centre, and the signature, and it was sent only to some public security stations, as we see.
